records.name: Taraba
records.current_summary:
Taraba sits under Nigeria's federal criminal law: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises arranging, attending or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups. August 2026 foreign travel guidance warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation anywhere in the country. The same reporting era records mass arrests and detentions of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in northern states, and the August 2024 beating death of a widely followed transgender content creator in the federal capital, hours after a public post, with the murder left unsolved.

Some northern states add Sharia criminal provisions that can reach death-penalty outcomes; the audited sources do not place Taraba among the states applying them, and no Taraba-specific finding is documented either way. The visitor's profile here is the federal one: criminalisation on the statute book, arbitrary enforcement, and little protection against mob or individual violence.

sources.claim: Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026): the UK foreign office's travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation in Nigeria - same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years federally, and some northern states' Sharia law prescribes the death penalty for it; the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups; the advisory also warns that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The English Wikipedia page 'LGBT rights in Nigeria' sets out the federal framework under which Taraba sits: same-sex sexual activity has been illegal since 1904 in the Northern Region and since 1916 region-wide, and penalty is up to 14 years' imprisonment under federal law, the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act 2014 criminalising all forms of same-sex unions as well as registering or publicly promoting gay organisations. The page lists harsher Sharia-law penalties (from lashing or caning up to death) only for states that have adopted Sharia; Taraba is not named among them, matching this record's finding that no Taraba Sharia application is documented. The page contains no Taraba-specific statute or incident; it serves as the national-framework document the state's visitor stands under.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's report of 20 October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act', records that the SSMPA, signed into law on 7 January 2014, imposes prison terms of 10 to 14 years on anyone who operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and finds that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. The report is national in scope and names no Taraba-specific case, but it substantiates the federal criminalisation and arbitrary-enforcement climate on which Taraba's visitor assessment rests.

records.name: Ebonyi
records.current_summary:
Ebonyi is governed by the federal provisions the audited sources document for Nigeria: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups; a national feature on queer life under those laws (retrieved as a fetch-time summary) reports threats and raids alongside informal community organising, and foreign-government travel guidance warns LGBT+ visitors of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation.

No Ebonyi-specific statute, enforcement action, or protection is identified in the sources examined. The state is therefore assessed at the national position: criminalisation on the books, a hostile enforcement climate, and no documented local divergence in either direction.

sources.claim: NOTE: page content was site navigation only at fetch time; the underlying August 2026 feature (per its URL slug) covers Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: National-framework document for West Nusa Tenggara: Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, and in December 2022 Parliament passed a new Penal Code that criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison and complaints admissible from immediate family, a provision set to take effect on 2 January 2026 - the code the record's first claim references. The page also records that in Aceh homosexuality is illegal under sharia law with flogging or imprisonment, that police raids on 'gay parties' continue (75 people arrested at a private villa near Jakarta on 22 June 2025, plus raids in South Jakarta in February and May 2025), that conversion therapy is widely practiced, and that 93% of Indonesians labelled homosexuality 'morally unacceptable' in Pew data cited for 2025. It does not name West Nusa Tenggara specifically; it is the encompassing national framework under which the province stands.

sources.title: West Nusa Tenggara - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The province's own page: West Nusa Tenggara consists of the two large islands of Lombok and Sumbawa, has an estimated population of 5,731,110 (mid-2025 official estimate), and is overwhelmingly Muslim - 96.88% per 2022 Ministry of Religious Affairs data - with Islam documented as the official religion of the region's historical kings. The majority Sasak people of Lombok preserve strong traditions ('Wetu Telu', a form of Islam influenced by local beliefs), and the page stresses the provinces' conservative religious character and tourism-dependent economy. It contains no LGBT-specific statute or incident, but it documents the demographic and cultural setting - the record's 'Lombok culture' claim - in which the province's LGBT-related bylaws and the national Penal Code's morality provisions operate.

records.name: Banten
records.current_summary:
The audited sources for Banten are national-level and were only partly retrievable: a 2022 wire report on police denying mistreatment after a foreign transgender activist died on drug charges in Bali custody (page unretrievable; fetch-time summary), and an August 2026 feature on growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community (navigation-only at fetch; headline and dossier summary).

No Banten-specific statute, ordinance, raid, protection or service is documented in anything examined. A visitor in Banten therefore stands under the national picture those sources sketch - no criminalisation of gender identity itself, rising official and vigilante hostility toward LGBT+ visibility, and weak accountability for mob violence - but this record asserts nothing beyond that shared, hedged base.

sources.claim: NOTE: page content was site navigation only at fetch time; the underlying August 2026 feature (per its URL slug) covers Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The article records that since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identity papers (including the e-KTP), and it names Banten among the nine provinces whose transgender residents have benefited so far (with West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua); the stated reasoning was that many of those people were undocumented, especially where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans visitor standing under the national framework in Banten, this documents that the province is one of the nine where identity-document issuance for transgender people has operated since mid-2021, which bears on document status and enrolment for trans travellers in this division.

sources.claim: NOTE: page content was site navigation only at fetch time; the underlying August 2026 feature (per its URL slug) covers Indonesia's transgender community facing growing repression.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia – Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national-framework article on LGBTQ rights in Indonesia, which applies throughout the country including this province, records that since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), with only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors recognised and birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained, and that electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces. It records that the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage is set to take effect on 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison, and that because same-sex marriage is not legally recognised, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. It further notes that transgender identity (waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture, alongside documented repressive incidents including raids on transgender women by the Jakarta Social Agency and the January 2021 flogging of two men in Aceh province (BBC/Reuters). This is the national-framework evidence for the record's assessment that a visitor in this province stands under Indonesia's national position: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X-marker, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after its enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. It also records international criticism, including from the United Nations, for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships. This is the national statutory framework, effective from 2 January 2026, under which a visitor in this province stands for the record's no-deviation assessment.

sources.claim: The Diplomat feature (Aug 2026): vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia in a 14-16 July 2026 wave, including over 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor with footage shared online; an October 2025 presidential decree lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; legal gender change requires sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval; provincial moral laws and Aceh caning remain the enforcement texture; a researcher documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia
sources.claim: National framework page (applies to West Kalimantan, which records no separate regulation; the national position is what a visitor stands under). Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected 5-4 a conservative petition seeking to criminalise homosexuality and extramarital sex, declining to add them to the Penal Code. Transgender Indonesians who do not hide their identity often struggle to keep legitimate employment and can be pushed into sex work; a global survey cited on the page reports discrimination and harassment are not uncommon though direct violence is rare. The West Kalimantan division page records no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement, so the national framework governs.
